newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia euthanasia battle shifts ground after vote.
newsitem.headline: Australia euthanasia battle shifts ground after vote.

text.p: Australian euthanasia campaigners are preparing to take their battle to the country's autonomous states after the federal parliament killed off the Northern Territory's pioneering suicide law.

"This is not where the debate ends -- it just enters a different phase," pro-euthanasia senator Kate Lundy told the Senate as it voted to confirm a lower house bill overriding the Northern Territory's nine-month-old euthanasia law.
The vote rejected the views of the 75 percent of Australians who backed voluntary euthanasia for the terminally ill.
Almost as importantly, it also broke the strong constitutional convention that the federal government let the two self-governing territories look after their own affairs.

Although the self-governing territories elect their own legislatures they are constitutionally subordinate to the federal government -- unlike the six states, whose powers are determined by the national constitution, not by Canberra.
Lundy said a state's creation of a euthanasia law would not only bypass the federal parliament, it would pressure Canberra to end its prohibition on suicide in the territories.
"If a state moved to enact a euthanasia law it would be incumbent on the federal government to repeal the act," Lundy told Reuters.
Victoria is seen as the best hope. Victorian state Premier Jeff Kennett, a forceful politician who usually gets his own way, is a vocal supporter of voluntary euthanasia.
The Australian constitution reserves certain functions -- such as defence, trade and company law -- to the federal parliament, leaving everything else to the states.

If Canberra cannot find such a "head of power" to cover a law, it has to leave the subject to the states. So the general criminal law relating to murder and suicide, for example, is a state responsibility.

In the past, federal governments imaginatively managed to connect apparently unrelated issues to a head of power and the limits of federal authority are never certain. The High Court ruled in the 1980s, for example, that if Australia had signed an international environmental treaty then Canberra's external-affairs power gave it the right to prevent a state from damming a river.
Territory politicians were outraged on Tuesday at parliament's approval of the anti-euthanasia bill, which was sponsored by Christian conservative politician Kevin Andrews.

"Territorians will awake this morning to the news that they simply don't have the same rights that other Australians take for granted," Northern Territory Chief Minister Shane Stone told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
Prime Minister John Howard, who supported the bill in a free conscience vote, said euthanasia was a more important issue than the territories' constitutional status.

"I do think this is a case where views about the rights of the territories and the states -- which after all are only theories of government -- are far less important than conscientiously-held views about matters of life and death," he said.

Four people legally killed themselves while the territory law was in effect, using a computer-controlled machine that injected a lethal drug. The first was 66-year-old cancer sufferer Bob Dent, who used it in September to end what he called "a roller-coaster of pain".
